extracted.intended_audience: general readers, policymakers, researchers and practitioners interested in misinformation, media literacy, and regulation of fake news
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and analysis of fake news: its causes, historical examples, mechanisms of spread (bots, deepfakes, filter bubbles), and public-policy / behavioral interventions to detect, limit or punish misinformation. Includes legal responses, platform actions, cognitive and educational strategies (media literacy, nudges, inoculation/prebunking) and examples from countries and studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and criminal sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous countries have created laws in an attempt to regulate or prosecute harmful misinformation more generally than just with a focus on tech companies; people have been arrested for allegedly spreading fake news about the COVID-19 pandemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Algerian lawmakers passed a law criminalising 'fake news' deemed harmful to 'public order and state security'; Turkish Interior Ministry arrested social media users for posts 'targeting officials and spreading panic and fear'; Iran reported 3,600 arrests for 'spreading rumors'; Cambodia and the United Arab Emirates introduced arrests or criminal penalties related to COVID-19 misinformation. Note the practical difficulty of prosecuting anonymously hosted fake news websites for libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platforms can be compelled or required to remove content
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and regulators can mandate removal or blocking of content on platforms when postings are defamatory or otherwise unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: An Austrian court issued an injunction requiring Facebook Europe to block negative postings related to a politician (Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek). This demonstrates legal remedies can target platforms as intermediaries for content removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform policies and enforcement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tech companies implement policies and enforcement measures (e.g., suspensions, removals, spending on counter-misinformation) to combat fake news and misinformation on their services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Google allocated funding to combat fake news; YouTube suspended One America News Network (OANN) for spreading coronavirus misinformation and deleted a video promoting a guaranteed cure. Twitter implemented 'read before you retweet' prompts. Facebook changed terminology from 'fake news' to 'false news' and has taken deletion and account removal actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive biases of recipients (attention and sharing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information overload means humans cannot process all items; confirmation bias and other cognitive biases determine which information units people attend to and share, amplifying fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms and social media bots exploit these vulnerabilities by surfacing content users are likely to prefer. Research examples: study by Randy Stein showing conservatives value personal stories more than liberals (potentially affecting receptivity to scientific evidence), though that study tested apolitical messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nudges as reflection prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief prompts that nudge users to consider the accuracy of incoming information increase reflection, improve judgment accuracy, and reduce unreflective sharing of incorrect information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology-based example: Twitter's 'read before you retweet' prompt that encourages readers to open and consider article contents before retweeting. Empirical studies cited show nudging helps prompt accuracy considerations and reduces sharing of misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media literacy (critical media literacy education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching critical media literacy skills for printed and digital media helps readers self-evaluate the accuracy of content and is presented as an effective method to mitigate propaganda and fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nolan Higdon argues for a critical media literacy education focused on teaching critical thinking about how to detect fake news. Media literacy programs aim to teach verification, source evaluation, and skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental immune health, inoculation and prebunking
rubrics_metrics.description: Inoculation theory and prebunking aim to build public resilience (a 'mental immunity') to misinformation by pre-exposing people to weakened versions of misinformation and explaining the tactics and fallacies used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prebunking = debunking lies, tactics or sources before they strike. Examples: Google implemented prebunking video adverts shown effective in trials; John Cook's climate-change inoculation lists common myths, deconstructs reasoning errors and uses parallel argumentation (often with humour) to show flaws. Research supports inoculation for countering science denialism and other manipulative messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoculation two-step debunking method
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical inoculation method involves (1) listing and deconstructing common myths by identifying reasoning errors and logical fallacies, and (2) using parallel argumentation to transplant the flawed logic into an extreme or absurd situation to reveal the flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding appropriate humour can increase effectiveness. Example application: countering climate change denialism by deconstructing ~50 common myths and using parallel argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deepfakes and synthetic media risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Deepfakes are AI-generated synthetic media that replace a person's likeness in images or videos and have high potential to deceive; they are used for political fake news, child sexual abuse material, celebrity pornographic videos, revenge porn, hoaxes, bullying, and financial fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creation methods include deep learning architectures such as autoencoders and GANs. Responses include industry and government detection and limitation efforts. Note: shallowfakes (edited with standard software) can achieve similar deceptive effects with obvious flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shallowfakes (non-AI editing) also deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: Shallowfakes—videos edited with standard video software—may have obvious flaws but can still be widely believed or have entertainment value that reinforces beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The Hillary Song' paste-in video that went viral. Shallowfakes require less specialist knowledge than deepfakes and can spread widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bots on social media amplify fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated accounts (bots) can mass-produce and spread articles without regard to credibility, create fake accounts and personas, and significantly contribute to the spread of misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bots use algorithms to select content users will like, increasing spread; almost 30% of spam and content spread originates from software bots. Examples include Russian troll farms paid to circulate fake news during elections; bots have been linked to major fake-news proliferation on Facebook and Twitter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter bubbles and personalization effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmic personalization (filter bubbles) delivers information tailored to user preferences, which can create biased exposure and reinforce fake or partial narratives by showing only the portions of stories a viewer likes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concept predicted by Nicolas Negroponte; filter bubbles interact with political polarization to increase tendencies to read headlines and share sensational content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-check visibility and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact checks of fake news are rarely seen by consumers; studies show consumers exposed to fake news are often not reached by related fact checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: fact checks of fake news were rarely seen and none of those who saw a fake news story were reached by a related fact check in certain studies. This reduces corrective impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/sensational content spreads more
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news often panders to expectations or is more exciting than legitimate news, which increases sharing and virality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts found fake news had higher sharing rates because it often meets emotional or expectation-based appeals. Facebook initially denied that fake news influenced elections despite research showing differential spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake news as a profit-driven enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Many 21st-century fake news operations are economically motivated, producing sensationalist stories to maximize clicks and advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Disinfomedia employed dozens of writers and reported monthly revenues of $10,000–$30,000 from advertisements. Google AdSense and social sharing can financially underpin fake-news sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trolling and coordinated disinformation campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet trolls and coordinated operations sow discord and spread misleading information; trolling can be done for amusement, political influence, or financial gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trolling takes many forms (abuse trolling, entertainment trolling, flame trolling, etc.). Notable example: Russia paid over 1,000 trolls in 2016 to circulate fake news and create convincing social media accounts targeted at swing-state voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and audience patterns of fake-news consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumption and sharing patterns vary by demographic groups: studies found older Americans and certain political audiences consumed and shared more fake news than others; high-volume consumers tend to be a small fraction of overall users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A 2019 study found users over 65 were more likely to share fake-news articles (11%) than those 18–29 (3%). Other studies found Trump supporters consumed the largest volume of junk news on Facebook and Twitter; fake-news audiences also often consume mainstream news sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical continuity of misinformation and propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news and propaganda have long historical precedents, used in ancient, medieval, and modern eras to influence opinion, foment violence, or sway political events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative instances: Mark Antony, Ramesses the Great, medieval blood libels, Great Moon Hoax (1835), yellow journalism in the 1890s, wartime atrocity propaganda, Nazi propaganda apparatus. This history contextualizes contemporary phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and international counter-disinformation mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: States and international bodies have established centers, codes of practice, and co-regulatory schemes to combat disinformation and protect information integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Centre Against Terrorism and Hybrid Threats (Czech Republic), European Commission's 2018 voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation (moving toward strengthened co-regulation alongside the Digital Services Act). International meetings planned for centers to combat disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy trade-offs and censorship concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to combat fake news raise concerns about censorship and 'thought police'; interventions must balance combating disinformation with protecting free expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Czech president Miloš Zeman criticized the creation of a government agency to fight disinformation, warning against censorship. Policy design must consider democratic norms and risks of overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: State incentives like 'reward and punish' systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Some governments propose incentive-based systems (rewards and punishments) to reduce spread of fake news, reflecting state-level policy experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: China's Ren Xianling suggested a 'reward and punish' system to avoid fake news. Such approaches illustrate a range of coercive and incentive-based policy tools used internationally.
